newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ayalas to go into infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ayalas to go into infrastructure.

text.p: The Philippines' largest conglomerate Ayala Corp is set to expand its business empire by investing in infrastructure-related projects, Ayala chairman Jaime Zobel de Ayala said on Tuesday.

"We have been greatly encouraged by the chance to expand our core businesses into new terrain. We have looked at the opportunities. We have weighed the risks and challenges. And we have chosen to be engaged," Ayala told a group of businessmen.
He said the new investments in areas such as transportation, roads and water services, would complement its existing businesses.
Ayala said the company had already invested in an elevated mass rail transit project which would pass through Manila's main thoroughfare.
It had also submitted an unsolicited proposal to build a $461-million railway that will connect Manila to its southern neighbours, Laguna and Batangas.
It had also expressed interest in joining the privatisation of Manila's water supply system.
Ayala further said its banking subsidiaries, Bank of the Philippine Islands and its investment banking arm BPI Capital Corp would put up a venture capital company.
It had invited eight local companies to join the venture capital firm, he said.

"It will take years to reap the dividends (of these projects). But we believe there is ample dividend enough in the impact of modern infrastructure on the economy as a whole -- for this will not fail to yield returns for our core businesses in the group," he said.
The conglomerate's flagship Ayala Land Inc is the leader in the real estate sector.
It also has stakes in the telecommunications, food manufacturing, insurance and information technology.
"The Ayala Group is harnessing its capabilities as a group of companies to bring to bear a synergistic approach to private sector involvement in economic development," he said.
Ayala said the country's current economic boom can be sustained if the policies of deregulation and liberalisation were continued.
"Philippine development can be sustained if we can maintain these policies of reform and institutionalise rigour in their implementation," said Ayala, a doyen among Filipino industrialists.

"In exactly the same way that we have climbed out of the hole of the stagnation, so will we continue to move forward -- through the liberalisation and privatisation of economic effort. Only these can ensure the continued overall growth in our economy," he added.
